summary: Defines the PLAIN SASL mechanism, a simple clear-text user and password method for use together with confidentiality from a lower layer such as TLS in protocols that lack a simple password command. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: PLAIN is a SASL login method that sends a username and password in one message. It does not protect that message, so the connection must already have suitable protection such as TLS.

subtitle: A single-message username and password mechanism for SASL that needs protection from another layer.

tldr.problem: Some application protocols need a simple username and password login but do not define a clear-text login command.
tldr.mechanism: PLAIN sends a UTF-8 message containing an optional authorization identity, an authentication identity and a clear-text password separated by NUL characters.
tldr.outcome: PLAIN provides no integrity or confidentiality itself, so implementations should use it only with adequate protection such as TLS. RFC 4616 updates RFC 2595 and was updated by RFC 8996.

facts.label: Message components
facts.value: authzid, authcid and passwd, separated by NUL

facts.label: Maximum accepted length for each part

today: RFC 4616 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2006 and was updated by RFC 8996. It updates RFC 2595, replacing Section 6.

sections.title: Why Use a Plain Password Mechanism
sections.content:
Clear-text passwords are simple and work with many existing authentication databases. PLAIN gives protocols without a simple password command a SASL mechanism for sending these credentials.

PLAIN does not provide its own security layer or protect integrity and confidentiality. The RFC intends it to be used with data security from another layer, generally TLS, and says implementations SHOULD NOT offer or use it by default without adequate protection.
sections.plainLanguage: PLAIN gives a protocol a simple way to send a username and password. It is safe only when another layer protects the connection.

sections.title: The PLAIN Client Message
sections.content:
The client sends one UTF-8 string containing an optional authorization identity, a NUL character, an authentication identity, another NUL character, and the clear-text password. The authorization identity says who the client wants to act as; the authentication identity names whose password it uses.

The server MUST accept each part up to 255 octets. NUL cannot appear inside any part because it separates them. If the client omits the authorization identity, the server derives it from the credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: The message has three parts separated by NUL characters: the identity to act as, the identity being authenticated, and the password. The first part may be omitted.

sections.title: How the Server Checks Credentials
sections.content:
The server checks the authentication identity and password against its authentication database. It also checks that those credentials allow the client to act as the requested or derived authorization identity. Both checks must succeed for authentication to succeed.

Strings are prepared before comparison. SASLprep is RECOMMENDED but not mandatory, so a server may use another preparation method or none to interoperate with an external system. If preparation fails or produces an empty string, verification fails.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks the password and then checks whether that user may act as the requested identity. If either check fails, authentication fails.

sections.title: Example Exchanges
sections.content:
The RFC shows PLAIN used after a client starts TLS and the server advertises the mechanism. In one example, the client sends an empty authorization identity, its authentication identity and password, and the server accepts the login.

A second example supplies one identity to act as and a different identity whose password is used. The server refuses the request because the credentials do not authorize that action.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show a login that succeeds when the credentials are valid and a request to act as another identity that the server rejects.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
PLAIN provides no confidentiality or integrity protection. Implementations SHOULD NOT advertise or use it without adequate external protection such as TLS. IETF specifications that list PLAIN as an applicable mechanism MUST require support for a strong data security service.

Even with TLS, the server learns the password and could reuse it to impersonate the user at other services that share that password. The RFC encourages clients to provide an operating mode that disables mechanisms likely to reveal the password to the server.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS can protect the password while it travels, but the server still learns it. Use PLAIN only with a protected connection and a trusted server.

viz.caption: ABNF FOR THE PLAIN CLIENT MESSAGE (RFC 4616)

data.title: Message structure
data.code:
message = [authzid] UTF8NUL authcid UTF8NUL passwd
UTF8NUL = %x00
